items.text: Today, we will be discussing education from a global perspective.  This basically means that we will be taking a big step back, and looking at research on how different countries perform academically, how they differ from each other, and what the consequences are of this kind of research.
items.question: How might examining global education differences impact our understanding of academic performance?
items.answer: We will be looking at how different countries perform academically and the consequences of this research. This global perspective allows us to understand educational variations and their implications.

items.text: We will start by talking about why we do international comparisons, discuss some of the general findings from recent data, point out some interesting patterns, and then finally, talk about some of the known consequences of doing these large-scale international comparisons.
items.question: What are the potential consequences of conducting large-scale international comparisons?
items.answer: We will talk about some of the known consequences of doing these large-scale international comparisons.

items.text: So why do we do these large-scale international comparisons?  Well, these studies are conducted in order to compare different countries’ educational systems, specifically in terms of their structure and how effective they are. By making these differences clear, we can better understand the structural factors associated with good performance. This can then be used to inform educational reform efforts.  Finally, comparing achievement data can help us better understand the psychological mechanisms underlying learning.
items.question: How can international comparisons of educational systems inform reform efforts and our understanding of learning mechanisms?
items.answer: These studies clarify structural differences in educational systems and their effectiveness. This understanding can guide educational reforms and reveal psychological mechanisms of learning.

items.text: There are two prominent sets of data that are collected on an international basis: PISA and TIMSS.  PISA, or the Program for International Student Assessment, is administered every 3 years, and measures 15 year olds’ reading, mathematics, and science literacy. PISA emphasizes functional skills that students have acquired through schooling.  For example, PISA tends to ask questions about how academic concepts apply to real life.  This happens to be a strength of this data because these literacy-based comparisons are not dependent on specific curricula, and therefore are always valid internationally.  However, one weakness is that the data cannot yield any information about how the curriculum and educational systems of the participating countries specifically influence achievement. TIMSS, or the Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study, has measured the mathematics and science achievement of fourth and eighth grade students for the past 20 years.  The TIMSS assessment data is collected every 4 years, and is curriculum-based.  This happens to be a major strength because the curriculum differences between countries become transparent when data are analyzed.  This is something that PISA data is unable to provide.  However, one weakness is that the data may not reflect relevant competences for real life, or real literacy-based skills.
items.question: How do PISA and TIMSS differ in their approach to assessing student achievement?
items.answer: PISA emphasizes functional skills and real-life applications, while TIMSS focuses on curriculum-based assessments of mathematics and science achievement.

items.text: Ok, so now that we know what the data is and where it comes from, we will discuss some of the general findings from these international datasets.  This graph shows data from the most recent wave of PISA. You can see who the top performers are by looking at the top of the list.  Shanghai-China appears to be on the top in both mathematics and sciences, followed by Singapore.  In math, several other Asian countries, including Hong Kong and Korea are also top performers, about 50 points or more above average.   In terms of science literacy, Finland and New Zealand do very well, with scores about 30 to 50 points above average. Overall, international comparison data tells us where countries stand relative to one another, and reveal a tendency for some East Asian countries to be at the top.
items.question: What do the international datasets reveal about the performance of East Asian countries in education?
items.answer: International comparison data shows that East Asian countries, particularly Shanghai-China and Singapore, are top performers in mathematics and sciences.

items.text: Now, let’s move on to the second part of the lesson, and discuss some of the interesting patterns that can be found in the data.  One important question that has been raised is whether or not good performance comes at a hefty price.  Well, for a long time, psychologists believed that students’ positive attitudes toward learning and/or self-perceptions of their competence positively influences academic achievement.  However, recently, this link has been questioned with the emergence of international comparative data.  That is because these data have consistently shown that countries that do well in math and science, particularly some of the east Asian countries, also happen to score the lowest in both confidence in their abilities and enjoyment of the subjects.  This is an irony that has been labeled as the ‘attitude-achievement paradox’.  You can see from this table, that countries where students report having high confidence in math also happen to be below the international average in terms of achievement.  On the other hand, countries with the fewest students being confident in math happen to be the highest achievers.
items.question: What does the 'attitude-achievement paradox' reveal about the relationship between confidence and academic performance in different countries?
items.answer: The 'attitude-achievement paradox' reveals that countries with high academic achievement often have low confidence and enjoyment in subjects like math and science.

items.text: A similar trend exists in terms of liking math and achievement in math, where countries that report to like math the most have the lowest achievement scores in math, and countries that report to like math the least have the highest achievement scores.
items.question: How might a country's attitude towards math influence its students' achievement in the subject?
items.answer: Countries that report liking math the most have the lowest achievement scores, while those that like it the least have the highest scores.

items.text: This international attitude-achievement paradox is extensively discussed in literature.  Tom Loveless, for example, has found that national indices of student happiness are inversely related to achievement in mathematics.  Specifically, countries with more confident students who like math do not do as well as countries that rank lower on these attitudinal measures. This leaves us with the question: Why does this happen?
items.question: What might explain the paradox of student happiness and achievement in mathematics across different countries?
items.answer: The paradox suggests that higher student happiness and confidence in math do not correlate with better achievement. This raises the question of why this occurs.

items.text: While there are many hypotheses about this, three major explanations dominate the field:  Modesty bias, translation error, and academic pressure. We will now go into each of these in more detail.
items.question: What are the three major explanations mentioned that dominate this field?
items.answer: The three major explanations are modesty bias, translation error, and academic pressure.

items.text: Literature on modesty bias claims that students from some cultures, especially east Asian cultures, may be more likely to be modest in their responses and not endorse extreme values. This leads them to answer towards the center of a scale (usually 4-point Likert type scale) more so than people from other cultures.
items.question: How might cultural influences shape students' responses on surveys, particularly regarding modesty bias?
items.answer: Students from some cultures, especially east Asian cultures, may exhibit modesty bias by responding more conservatively on scales. This results in them favoring central responses rather than extreme values.

items.text: Another potential explanation is imprecision in translating questionnaires into other languages.  Researchers believe that this happens rather frequently, and can produce inaccurate results since the questionnaires may convey slightly different meanings across cultures. For instance, the anchor statements for the points on the attitude rating scales may be worded slightly stronger or weaker depending on the language, which could influence the responses people give.
items.question: How might language differences affect the accuracy of questionnaire results in research?
items.answer: Imprecision in translating questionnaires can produce inaccurate results, as meanings may vary across cultures. This can influence responses due to differently worded anchor statements.

items.text: The final explanation of the attitude-achievement paradox is that high academic pressure can compromise students’ levels of confidence in math abilities, as well as their enjoyment of it.  Particularly, higher achieving Asian countries, such as Korea and Japan, tend to have more demanding curricula, higher academic standards, and more pressure to achieve, which in turn can lead to less enjoyable learning experiences in school.  And, this can lower students’ self-concept, or perceived competence.
items.question: How does academic pressure affect students' confidence and enjoyment in math, particularly in high-achieving countries?
items.answer: High academic pressure can compromise students’ confidence in math abilities and their enjoyment of the subject. This is particularly evident in higher achieving Asian countries with demanding curricula.

items.text: So far, we learned about some of the reasons for conducting international comparisons as well as some interesting scientific investigations that can come out of this data.  Now, we're going to talk about what kind of impact these comparisons can have on participating countries.  To do this, we’re going to focus on the impact of international comparisons on educational reform in one specific country: Germany.
items.question: How might international comparisons influence educational reform in Germany?
items.answer: International comparisons can provide insights and data that inform educational reforms. This discussion will specifically focus on the impact of these comparisons on Germany.

items.text: Here’s the graph of math literacy from PISA data taken in year 2000. This data showed that Germany was doing average at best in comparison to other countries. This came as quite a shock to Germany because they considered their education system to be effective and of high quality, and the underlying reason behind country’s financial success.
items.question: What does the PISA data reveal about Germany's perception of its education system versus its actual performance in math literacy?
items.answer: The PISA data showed that Germany was doing average at best in comparison to other countries. This was surprising to Germany, which believed its education system was effective and high quality.

items.text: This lower than expected performance overall led to the realization of another relevant factor in student achievement: In Germany, student performance was found to be VERY strongly tied to socioeconomic status and migration background, more so than a majority of other countries. This meant that there was a great deal of difference in how well the rich and the poor, the immigrants and the citizens did. This led to an investigation as to why there might be such inequality in performance, which concluded that it may have something to do with the German educational system.
items.question: How does socioeconomic status influence student performance in Germany compared to other countries?
items.answer: In Germany, student performance is very strongly tied to socioeconomic status and migration background. This disparity led to an investigation into the educational system's role.

items.text: In Germany, there are different types of secondary education that children can receive. Those who do very well academically can go to the schools with a very high academic focus, the Gymnasium schools. Upon graduation, these students go on to university and form the more highly educated sector of society. On the other hand, there are schools with a very low academic focus, the Haupthschule schools. Students with average or below average grades attend these schools. While it is possible for these students to attend university after graduation, it is very rare. There is also a third type of school that falls somewhere in the middle, the Realschule schools. This system of schooling was meant to be academically selective, with the best students going to the best schools. However, the system also ended up being very socially selective, where the best schools have a significant overrepresentation of wealthy students and those without a migration history. So, with the most privileged children attending the best schools, it became less surprising that factors like SES had so much to do with the performance of German students on international comparison tests.
items.question: How does the German secondary education system reflect social privilege and academic performance?
items.answer: The German secondary education system is academically selective, but it also becomes socially selective, favoring wealthy students. This leads to disparities in performance on international tests.

items.text: In addition to the social disparity in achievement, the PISA data highlighted some other shortcomings of the German educational system. In particular, German schools had relatively large class sizes and relatively short school days. Additionally, there was a generally low rate of students attending higher education institutions, and little money was spent on education, both in terms of public and private funding.
items.question: What are the key shortcomings of the German educational system highlighted by the PISA data?
items.answer: The PISA data highlighted large class sizes, short school days, low higher education attendance, and insufficient funding for education in Germany.

items.text: So, in sum, the international comparison data revealed that Germany was performing at very average levels relative to other countries, and that there was a lot of inequality and numerous other shortcomings of their educational system. Now that we fully understand what the data showed, we will see what actually happened in Germany as a reaction to this shocking news of their mediocre performance. In sum, the results of international comparisons led to 3 changes in Germany. First, it impacted the political discourse on education and reforming the educational system. Second, it impacted the academic curriculums of schools. And third, the academic discourse on education also changed as a reaction to this data.  We will now discuss each of these in a little more detail.
items.question: What were the three key changes in Germany's education system following the international comparison data?
items.answer: The results of international comparisons led to changes in political discourse on education, academic curriculums, and academic discourse on education.

items.text: The PISA results led to a demand for educational reform in the German political landscape. However, it was not done perfectly.  While the PISA data highlighted the inequality of the school system and various structural issues with schools, these reform efforts targeted very few of these areas directly. Instead, politicians focused on developing national standards in education, which were implemented rather quickly. Also, along with the national standards came national assessments to see whether these standards were being met. The educational reform also included various efforts to promote reading, math, and science abilities.  This included increasing the number of schools that offer all-day instead of just half-day schooling, and trying to improve the performance of students with a migration background by increasing understanding of other cultures.
items.question: What were the main focuses of the educational reforms in Germany following the PISA results?
items.answer: The reforms primarily targeted developing national standards and assessments, while also promoting reading, math, and science abilities.

items.text: Germany also felt that a reform of the curriculum was necessary.  With the implementation of national standards, teachers were encouraged to only use the national standards as a basis for their teaching. Unfortunately, the standards tend to be somewhat vague, idealistic and outcome-focused. They do not come with any guidance on how to implement them, which places the burden of finding ways to meet these standards on teachers. Many believe that this is likely to lead teachers to rely on textbooks to guide their teaching, so the quality of the books used will become more important. Overall, it has been argued that the lack of a focus on how to actually achieve national standards will make any curriculum reform less beneficial.
items.question: How might the vagueness of national standards impact teachers' approaches to curriculum reform?
items.answer: The vagueness of national standards places the burden on teachers to find ways to meet them. This may lead teachers to rely heavily on textbooks, affecting the quality of education.

items.text: Finally, international comparisons likely shifted the academic discourse on education as well.  First, it contributed to a shift from a general didactic orientation to a more empirical orientation, which is more focused on how schools actually are, rather than what they should be.  Second, with the new educational standards, the main goal of education now became performing well on tests rather than the learning-based goals that were emphasized before. This could be seen as harmful for learning, as a focus on learning itself takes a back seat to performance in this framework.
items.question: How did international comparisons influence the focus of education according to the passage?
items.answer: International comparisons shifted the focus from general didactic approaches to empirical ones, emphasizing test performance over learning-based goals.

items.text: Overall, the mediocre performance of German students in international comparisons highlighted some important shortcomings of the educational systems and stimulated changes to the political, academic, and social landscape of German education.  Some changes were good, while some were not so much.  For instance, while a focus on national standards, curriculums, and assessments developed out of the international comparison results, more fundamental issues within the educational system were largely ignored. The changes they did decide to make may have some positive and negative consequences as discussed, and whether or not these reform efforts will have a great impact in the long run will be interesting to see. As such, the foundation of reform efforts in Germany and other countries came from revelations from the international comparison data.  This suggests the powerful impact that these data can have, not only in academia but in political contexts as well.
items.question: How did international comparisons influence educational reforms in Germany, and what were some consequences of these changes?
items.answer: The mediocre performance of German students highlighted shortcomings in the educational system, stimulating changes that had both positive and negative consequences.
